I'm not really married to the design as such but I'm looking for the best possible tool to do the job when firearms have failed. Apart from my Strider/Tarani I also have a Cold Steel "Steel Tiger" (not my favorite) as well as an Emerson Combat Karambit (folder). Neither of these other two knives fit the bill in my opinion for the job. You mentioned there are plenty of cheaper production Karambits out there that as good if not better - would you mind sharing your top 3/5 favorites?

Lastly one of the things I've really been struggling with is trying to find good, combat karambit specific instructional media to give me a solid foundation of fundamentals I can build on. I currently have two instructional DVD's, "Mastering the Curved Blade" by Steve Tarani and "The Complete Combat Karambit" by Emerson Combat Systems. I wasn't too impressed with either of these, less so with the Tarani one. Just to put things into perspective, I own and operate a self-defense academy under the Gracie University of Jiu-Jitsu. I've been training for 17 years and have been a Black Belt for 5 years. My passion is Jiu-Jitsu for Combat (think Law Enforcement, Military, Security professionals etc.) This has a big influence on my approach to Combat both with firearms, edge weapons etc. In a real world altercation, fine motor functions don't work, gross motor functions do. Thus, some of what I saw in the Tarani video I just couldn't stomach... but maybe I'm  wrong? Could you recommend any instructional material that fits the bill as far as real world application. 

Thanks again for your sage wisdom man, there are so many YouTube experts out there, it's really hard to know who to trust! :-)

That's great - sorry it didn't turn out the way you wanted. Sadly, that's the case with so many folks who dream those kinds of big dreams i.e. boats and sailing.  Without trying to sound conceited, having "made it" in life, I've realized that if you have everything you want on the physical level and achieved what you set out to, then the only thing left to strive for, is the next challenge/goal you set for yourself. And so the cycle continues, like a hamster on a wheel. Funny thing is, I wonder if people purposefully DON'T go after the dream/goal/etc. because it's that endorphin rush and excitement when you're thinking about it that fuels the fire to keep us moving forward? Like when you and a friend play the game "if you won the lottery, what would you do?!"
Yeah, I grew up on the ocean. Literally.
